claim: The relative occupancies of GTFs are consistent across all yeast promoters and quantitatively linked to transcriptional activity.

claim: A structurally similar PIC mediates a given level of transcription in yeast.

claim: A structurally similar PIC is responsible for most transcription in mammalian cells.

claim: TAFs are not required for transcription in vitro.

claim: TAFs are often components of the PIC in vivo.
source: TBP-associated factors (TAFs), which together with TBP constitute the TFIID complex, are not required for transcription in vitro, but they are often components of the PIC in vivo.

claim: In yeast cells, TAF occupancies are strongly correlated with each other.

claim: In yeast cells, TAF occupancies do not strictly correlate with TBP occupancy.

source: Thus, transcription in yeast cells can be mediated by PICs with TAF-containing (TFIID) or TAF-lacking forms of transcriptionally active TBP.

claim: The relative usage of TAF-containing and TAF-lacking PIC forms depends on the promoter and the quality of the TATA sequence.
source: The relative usage of these two PIC forms depends on the promoter and the quality of the TATA sequence (Struhl, 1986; Iyer and Struhl, 1995; Moqtaderi et al., 1996; Basehoar et al., 2004; Huisinga and Pugh, 2004; Petrenko et al., 2019) as well as the activator protein that stimulates PIC formation (Li et al., 2002; Mencia et al., 2002).

claim: The relative usage of TAF-containing and TAF-lacking PIC forms depends on the activator protein that stimulates PIC formation.

evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: The TAF-lacking form of TBP may be associated with the SAGA complex via the Spt3 subunit.
source: The TAF-lacking form of TBP may be associated with the SAGA complex via the Spt3 subunit (Eisenmann et al., 1992; Bhaumik and Green, 2001; Larschan and Winston, 2001; Basehoar et al., 2004; Papai et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020), but there is no direct evidence that SAGA associates with the promoter in vivo.

claim: There is no direct evidence that SAGA associates with the promoter in vivo.
source: The TAF-lacking form of TBP may be associated with the SAGA complex via the Spt3 subunit (Eisenmann et al., 1992; Bhaumik and Green, 2001; Larschan and Winston, 2001; Basehoar et al., 2004; Papai et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020), but there is no direct evidence that SAGA associates with the promoter in vivo.

claim: Some metazoan tissues possess tissue-specific TAFs and tissue-specific TFIID subunit composition.
source: Some metazoan tissues possess tissue-specific TAFs and tissue-specific TFIID subunit composition (D'Alessio et al., 2009; Hart et al., 2009; Maston et al., 2012).

claim: There is no evidence for the existence of free TBP in metazoan cells.
source: There is no evidence for the existence of free TBP in metazoan cells, and it is unclear whether there are TAF-lacking, or perhaps SAGA-containing forms of transcriptionally active TBP.

claim: It is unclear whether there are TAF-lacking, or perhaps SAGA-containing forms of transcriptionally active TBP in metazoan cells.
source: There is no evidence for the existence of free TBP in metazoan cells, and it is unclear whether there are TAF-lacking, or perhaps SAGA-containing forms of transcriptionally active TBP.

claim: Fluorescent studies suggest that activity of Drosophila histone gene promoters might rely only on TBP and TFIIA in the absence of TFIIB and TAFs.

claim: Mediator is a large complex (21–30 proteins depending on the species) that interacts with Pol II.
source: Mediator is a large complex (21–30 proteins depending on the species) that interacts with Pol II, and it can stimulate PIC assembly, phosphorylation of the Pol II C-terminal domain (CTD) by TFIIH, and basal transcription in vitro (Thompson et al., 1993; Kim et al., 1994; Guidi et al., 2004; Takagi and Kornberg, 2006; Esnault et al., 2008).

claim: Mediator can stimulate PIC assembly, phosphorylation of the Pol II C-terminal domain (CTD) by TFIIH, and basal transcription in vitro.

source: The evolutionarily divergent tail module interacts with activator proteins bound at enhancers, whereas the highly conserved head and middle modules interact with Pol II.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Mediator structure and function.

claim: Mediator coincides with the PIC at enhancers in MM1S cells.

claim: There is a strong Pearson correlation (range 0.65–0.74) between Med1, Pol II, and TBP levels at the 10,000 most active mRNA promoters in human cells.
